Mr. Chairman, on the income tax resolutions and arising out of this first resolution, I would like to raise one question. This item deals with allowances in lieu of certain expenditures and refers among other things to trade union dues.
On the west coast and perhaps in other parts of Canada there has been a situation arise with regard to income tax which is very worrisome to the trade unions and which I submit could be dealt with by the government without any further delay and I believe without any amendment to legislation. I am referring to the practice which the Department of National Revenue has adopted in recent months of charging income tax on board and lodging of construction workers who are working away from their home centres.

In British Columbia there has been and is and will be a great deal of construction work going on in the more remote centres of the province which involves the removal of many thousands of our construction workers from their home centres out to these jobs. Unfortunately the department is taking the position that these men must pay income tax on the allowance that is made to them by the employer for board and lodging. Most of these men have their homes to maintain in Vancouver, Victoria or in other centres in the province. They have all these living expenses which of course are quite properly not deducted when income tax is being levied but where they have to go away and live for temporary periods the money they are paid for board and lodging should be deducted. They should not have to pay income tax on those particular amounts.
For a number of years it was understood that the law was such that they did not have to pay income tax on these amounts. For example, I understand that on August 13, 1942 Mr. C. F. Elliot, who was then commissioner of income tax, wrote to John W. Bruce, the general organizer of the United Association of Journeymen and Apprentices of the Plumbing and Pipefitting Industry of the United States and Canada concerning this question and his letter contained the following words:
However, If the employer instead pays the expenses of the employee while working out of town, the employee will only be taxed on the wages he receives and not on the expenses borne by the [DOT]employer.
That practice seems to have been followed for many years. It was in question in 1953, because I know I raised it myself in my speech on the budget on March 11, 19.53 and last July 10 the Department of National Revenue issued what it described as "Information Bulletin No. 10". The heading is "Subject: Taxation of per diem and other allowances" and the first two paragraphs of this bulletin read as follows:
This bulletin outlines the requirements of the Income Tax Act with reference to the taxation of per diem and other allowances paid to employees in various industries, but with particular reference to subsistence and commuting allowances paid in the construction industry.
The Income Tax Act requires that, with certain *exceptions, any amount paid to an employee as an "allowance" must be included in computing his income. In the circumstances with which this bulletin is concerned the only exception applicable is that which exempts from tax reasonable allowances for travelling expenses paid to a permanent employee for a period when he is performing his duties away from the municipality in which his employer's establishment at which he ordinarily works is located. In the majority of cases the periodic subsistence and commuting allowances commonly paid in the construction industry do not fall in the exempt category.
Income Tax Act
Now that means apparently that the act has been interpreted by the department or the taxation authorities to mean that if a construction superintendent who is on the permanent payroll of a company goes to Kitimat to superintend a construction job there and is paid or is given an allowance for his board and room while in Kitimat he does not have to pay any tax on that amount. On the other hand, the rest of the construction workers who are not on the payroll permanently- and as members know, very few construction workers in work of this type or jobs of this kind are on the payroll permanently- if they went up to Kitimat they would have to pay tax on such allowance as they received for board and lodging. I do submit, that is unfair and that these men should be treated in the same way, for example, as some groups who are exempt, such as railway employees and taxpayers in employment and whose principal business is in connection with passengers and goods transport and so on. This may just have been an oversight on the part of the department but we are now at a stage in the development of Canada when it is necessary for construction workers to go to remote places. I dare say in every single province of Canada that condition prevails and men will have to go, not only within the provinces but to the Northwest Territories and eventually probably into the Arctic islands, north of the mainland of Canada.
There should be no more delay in dealing with this question. The unions on the west coast have made representations, 1 think very reasonable representations, on the point and I have here as a matter of fact a brief presented by the Canadian Labour Congress on December 4, 1956 covering this point and I find that in their conclusion they have this to say:
Neither the construction employee nor employer is trying to avoid the payment of tax on income earned during the taxation year but for the reasons enumerated above emphatically deny that these out of town living expenses constitute income. They, therefore, respectfully ask that the act be amended to exempt the expenses of construction workers only from tax by an amendment in a form similar to the following:
"Reasonable allowances for travelling expenses and out of town living expenses received by an employee of a construction contractor while working on a construction project away from his normal place of residence."
Now that seems to me to be a very proper request. Actually I doubt whether it is necessary to have an amendment to the act. It seems to me that this point could be covered by a change in the regulations, or it may even be that the regulations are all right and merely that this information in bulletin No. 10 is all wrong. I hope that either the Minister of Finance or the Minister of National

Income Tax Act
Revenue will assure the committee today that this tax on these allowances is to be dropped.
I do not believe that there is any justification for levying this tax and it is a kind of tax that causes extremely bad feeling because some people do not have to pay it. As I pointed out, the construction superintendents do not have to pay it but the men under them do and this is a very bad situation to have existing in our taxation laws. Finally there is also the fact that this tax is making it more difficult for Canada to carry out construction jobs in the more remote parts of this country. I believe that the future of Canada depends primarily on the way and the speed with which we develop our north country and the more remote areas in the provinces. Certainly this tax, as it is being levied now, constitutes a great handicap to that development and a change should be made right away.

I would like to add my words to what has already been said by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra. In my period of occupation I have had actually only two jobs in my life, one in the construction industry and one in public services. On both I found I had to be away from home, so I can speak from almost a lifetime of experience on the principle which has been espoused and explained by the hon. member who spoke before me. Workers in the construction industry have on many occasions to leave their homes and take up employment many miles away. It may seem reasonable at first glance that if a man happens to be employed in an industry where his employer pays for his board, it should be included as part of income. But those who have actually been employed in construction work know they do not receive anything extra as a result of provision for their board being made, if they are normal persons; and most people are normal persons.
I remember when I was occupied solely in the construction industry, sometimes hundreds of miles away from home, I wanted to see my family and make arrangements either for them to visit me where I was working or to leave the job for a few days and go back home. In either case a worker loses some days on the job and, in addition, he has to pay costs of transportation. If it is right that because a construction worker away from home who is paid his board should have to pay tax on this amount, then it is also right that because he is separated from his family and wants to see them once in a while he should be granted consideration in respect of what he spends in so doing. But the national revenue department never thinks of that.
Along with the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra I was amazed when about a year

ago out of a blue sky, not because of any change in the law but as the result of regulations, a decision was reached that the amount received for board and lodging by construction workers away from home would be charged for the purpose of income tax. I think that is one of the most despicable things that has ever been done by way of regulation by the Department of National Revenue, and I am convinced that if a study were made of the position of a man or woman who is working away from home that regulation would be withdrawn after due consideration.
If the regulation is not withdrawn, then I think that all hon. members of this house who know something about the construction industry have the right to ask the Minister of Finance and the Minister of National Revenue to take into consideration the extra cost incurred by a person who is away from home in returning to see his family or in arranging for his family to see him. If this course is followed-and I think it is the decent thing to do-I believe hon. members will find that the cost of one will just about offset the cost of the other.
There is what is known in law as a question of doubt. Apparently it arises, in particular, in questions dealing with pensions and compensation. If we look at it only in this light, there is a question of doubt about what a man gains by being away from home and receiving an allowance as compared with what he loses, and what his family loses, because he is away. It is a question on which one could speak for a long time, but I wish to say this through you, Mr. Chairman, to the Minister of National Revenue and the Minister of Finance: some of the things they have done in the past are good, and some of the things are bad. But one of the rottenest things they ever did-not by way of law but by way of regulation-was to impose a burden on thousands of people in Canada by discriminating against those employed in the construction industry and saying that any allowance received by these workers when they leave home is going to be charged as income.
I am very happy, therefore, to give my support to what was said by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra and ask that this matter should be reconsidered, and that the regulation should be rescinded immediately.

Mr. Chairman, on behalf of the Social Credit group may I say that we would like very much to be associated with the words spoken by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra and others. Every hon. member of this house has in all likelihood received many resolutions with regard to this matter

and spent a great deal of time discussing the question with constituents engaged in the construction business.
It is a very simple matter indeed to deduct income tax from workers, and it is a very simple matter to introduce regulations which make that possible. However, the position is much more difficult for the contractors of this country who have the task of inducing men to leave their homes in order to carry out contract work away from city areas and travel into the interior of, for example, the province from which I come. It is much more difficult for contractors to do this than it is to keep men on the job within the cities.
It is easily understandable, as has been pointed out by hon. gentlemen who have spoken already, that it is not easy to keep men employed in outlying areas, especially if they find that they are not given the right to deduct their expenses and are to be charged for lodging and meals. I say this only because the minister should be made aware of the fact that all parties are in agreement, I think, with respect to this matter. I think he should take this into consideration and see if it would not be possible to change this regulation so as to make it possible for these men to remain on the job, because contractors find it so difficult at present to get men to leave their home areas and take up work elsewhere.
Could we have a statement from one of the ministers on this point?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, as everyone recognizes, this problem is not covered in the amendment before the house, and perhaps for that reason we should not spend too much time on it. I think it is recognized that this was brought about by administrative order and could be altered in the same manner. I do not think, therefore, that any amendment is required in the act.
I want to say at once, however, that this has been a very difficult matter to determine. There is no question but that the construction industry is unusual in this field, yet it is not wholly unique. There are other industries in which allowances for board and lodging are given. I think the best argument that could be made for the deductions that have been mentioned would be the matter of public need, in the sense that if the construction industry were not successful in doing those things that we wanted to do, and if the action which some hon. members have proposed were the means of avoiding that, we would have to give most serious consideration to what has been suggested.
On the other hand it ought to be clear that these benefits are real benefits to the taxpayer
Income Tax Act
and that it is necessary that the Department of National Revenue should fix some arbitrary rule for the imposition of the tax, because you will have one employer who will pay his working men, let us say $75 a week, all of which would be taxable as a wage.
You will then have another employer who will pay $50 a week by way of wages and $25 a week by way of allowance for board and lodging. You will have a third employer who will pay the $50 a week and provide the board' and lodging himself in camps and the like.
It is not easy to draw the proper rule as between all three or variations of them. We have been doing our best to find that thing which probably should not follow necessarily in any taxing law, namely a logical approach to everything. I do not think you can be wholly logical. However, we have been doing our best to find a rule which would tax everyone with the same kind of income unless there was a real case to be made for an exception. I think all hon. members of the committee would agree with me on that score, namely that if there are exceptions,-if I am being taxed for one thing that some hon. gentleman opposite is not being taxed for-there must be great justification for that exception to be made.
As I say, there is something to be said for everything that has been said here today. The construction industry may possibly be, by its very nature the exception to the rule that these benefits ought to be taxed. I agree with that proposition. I recognize that that is the best argument that can be made for the exemption that has been advocated. But I would hope that the committee would bear with me to this extent. If exemption is granted for this kind of income I think we want to see that two things will happen. We want to see that the income will be legitimate, that is to say that the amount set aside for board and lodging and fringe benefits, if I may put it that way, will not be out of proportion to what they ought to be so that the construction worker then will receive a tax exemption which no one else will receive. In the second place, we want to see that all other workers who are in about the same kind of situation will have their cases considered on their merits and we will be able to know where to draw the line with respect to the exemption, whether it should be drawn just at the construction workers or whether it should be extended beyond that.
This is not by any means an attempt to magnify the difficulties. I can assure you that they are real and troublesome. As for myself, I have not been able to suggest any other amendment to the law that there ought to be; nor for that matter have I been able to

Income Tax Act
satisfy myself that I should tell the maid in the house who pays income tax on her board and lodging that the construction worker ought not to do it because of the circumstances under which he works.
May I ask the minister a question?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Yes.
Does the minister consider that this matter comes within the scope of regulations?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Yes, there is no question about that. Regulations could be issued interpreting what should be done. I am satisfied on that point. If it turns out that I am wrong by any chance I am quite prepared to consider an amendment that might be made.
It merely requires a ministerial directive, does it not?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I think that is correct, as far as I know. But I place the case before the committee. I have not anything to add to what I have said. I think every hon. member will recognize the fact that the whole question of the taxation of fringe benefits is an extremely complex one and that, generally speaking, there ought not to be very much advantage to anyone in these things unless they are clearly understood and unless the exemption is understood and extends to all persons under like circumstances. I realize that hon. members may hold wholly different views from those that I hold. I think it is clear that I have no fixed view on this matter. However, I want a consistent tax law. For that reason all I can say is that at the moment I do not propose to make any amendment with respect to the matter. I think we ought to continue to study all these things, including transportation as well as just the board and lodging element of it, in an effort to have a consistent policy.
We have interviewed some of the gentlemen who have been mentioned by name already as representing the unions and we have interviewed the contractors as well in an effort to work out a suitable arrangement which would be agreeable not only to both employer and employee but would not prevent the recruiting of workmen for the more distant parts or for the more immediate parts as well. I have not been able to complete those discussions up until the present time. I feel that perhaps the house might bear with me for another short period of time. We may be able to do something.

There was one point with which the minister did not deal. I refer to the fact that the superintendent who goes

out on one of these construction jobs is not taxed on the allowances for board and lodging whereas the rest of the construction workers are so taxed. I quite agree with the minister that the taxation should be logical. However, it is extremely difficult to see anything logical about an arrangement of that kind. I submit that the two groups should be treated in the same way. If the superintendent gets his exemption, then the men working under him should also get it. The minister has brought in other industries. But I point out to him that this trouble arose only because there was a directive issued by the Department of National Revenue dealing exclusively with the construction industry.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: When conditions were entirely different from what they are today.
How do you mean?

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext:
Inasmuch as at the time
at which this directive was issued by Mr. Elliot to which my hon. friend referred it was not the practice for workers in Vancouver-if you want to take that city as an example-for instance, or in Sudbury to have employment in jobs outside of where they were resident to the extent that it is the practice today. The regulation has been there for a long while. Regulations are concurred in by privy council. It was last year that attention was drawn to the fact that the regulation was not being put into effect, and directive No. 10 was issued saying that it should be put into effect. I do not see anything very much wrong with it. I listened to the arguments that were advanced by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra. However, I know this. I investigated the matter personally. Up in the Sudbury district there has been a big rush from Sudbury to the uranium mines at Sprague.
Blind River.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext:
These fellows up there are
getting $20 to $25 a week extra to take that job. In addition to that they are getting increased rates in the particular job of work they are doing. For instance, if a fellow is a plumber, he gets a better rate per hour because of the fact he has gone to work with the Consolidated Denison construction group. In addition to that he gets $20. He pays only $2 a day or $14 a week out of that $20 a week which he gets. I asked the men themselves and they told me this. They pay $14 a week for their room and board; that is their bunk and their board. Therefore they are "in" to the extent of $6 a week.
I submit to you that the very fact they get the equivalent in money of their board and lodging, and in the instance which I have

cited an extra $6 a week, that that, in addition to the wage or the monthly wage or the hourly wage they are paid, is income in their hands and should be taxed.

Oh, yes, but that is not the
situation. Those men are paying tax on money that they get.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: Yes.

Nobody is complaining about
that. That is for wages. If they get a higher rate for going into that area for work, then they pay taxes on that higher rate.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: That is right.

And there is not any doubt
that they are entitled to get a good wage for going into work under those conditions. But the point is that the Department of National Revenue is taxing them on the allowances they get for board and lodging and that is what we are complaining about.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext:
That is the situation with
other people. For instance, the men who go into the bush are getting so much a month and they are paid the equivalent, which is low in these times, I think it is $30 a month for board. That is added on to their wages as part of their income for the year.
That may be so.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: And deductions at the source are made on that basis as if it had been in cash. I suggest to you that there is no difference between paying John Jones $100 per month and his board which, we will say is worth $30, and paying him $130 per month and asking him to pay $30 to the company for board.

But that can be handled by the department. They can decide what is a fair amount to be allowed for board and lodging. Neither minister has dealt with the fact that the superintendents, the men who are in charge, are getting this allowance and the other men are not. The directive to which I was referring was not a directive issued by Mr. Elliot, but this same directive No. 10. The trouble came up last year when the national revenue officials issued this directive No. 10; that is what made all the trouble. Before that, as I understand it, board and lodging were not being taxed, and that directive No. 10 only referred to the construction industry so that it is the construction industry that is being hurt.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
My hon. friend does not understand that the construction industry was the only one that was getting this tax exemption at that time; that is the point of the directive. Everybody else was being charged for board and lodgings, including the people in the bush.
Income Tax Act
The travelling salesmen are not.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I will come to that in a moment. That is the answer to my hon. friend's other question. Anyone whose income is fixed on the basis of his income plus his living allowance, with the exception of the construction workers, has been charged for both up to the present time, plus of course the proper determination of the value of the additional benefit. It was found last year that this did not apply to construction workers; that they were getting tax exemptions for their board and lodging. It was for that reason directive No. 10 was issued. I think, therefore, it can be fairly said, subject to what I am going to say in a moment, that now everyone who has a combined income of wages and benefits will be taxed for both.
Then my hon. friend asked why it is this does not apply in the case of the superintendent as well as the working man. The reason is given in the directive. This was an effort to extend the exemption again to those persons for whom a good case could be made, namely the permanent employee, for the reasons my hon. friend has just given that when a salesman goes around the country he is paid his expenses. He is a permanent employee and is someone you can trace in your business. He is a man who can be followed on the books of the company and by the nature of things he is doing something which improves the income of the firm for which he is working. He is on strength the year around, at least until he loses his job. He is a permanent expense, if you will. The case is the same with any permanent employee.
My hon. friend, I think with a little bit of malice perhaps, just used the word "superintendent" instead of permanent employee. This does not apply to the superintendent, it applies to every permanent employee. If there is a carpenter at Kitimat, as my hon. friend has said, who is a permanent employee of the construction company the year round he gets this advantage.
What is your definition of "permanent"?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I shall have to let the Minister of National Revenue give that.
Is it six months or a year or two years?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
As I say, I am only giving an expression of my own opinion, which then will be subject to the correct definition. I think a permanent employee is a person who, in the first instance, is hired for the purpose of working all the time. Some people work the year round for construction companies. It is true they will be laid off because

Income Tax Act
of temporary weather conditions but that is another matter. There are some people who hire themselves out by the season or go to a job for three months or four months at a time. They are not permanent employees. We have extended this exemption as wide as we could in order to be consistent by saying that anybody who is on the strength of the construction company the year round can have his exemption because his employer down in Vancouver may say you must go up to Kiti-mat to work for us. The employer does not say so, but the inference is if you do not we will have to hire someone else in your place. This does not apply to the mechanics, carpenters or other workmen who decide there is work to be had up there and who apply for a job for that period of time. They are a little different.
I know hon. members may say they are not different, but what I am trying to say is that the reason we have permanent employees in there getting the advantage of tax exemptions is because we think it is logical they should have that exemption as a great many people working in other lines of industry do have that exemption. We, therefore, gave it to them. The only chap we are quarrelling about is the chap who is hired for a job, so to speak, in the larger cities, and who is taken out to the job knowing that when the job is ended he is not going to have work unless the company hires him another year or for another job. As I say, that is the distinction about which we are talking this afternoon.
I repeat it might not be a distinction hon. gentlemen think ought to be made, but I think you can agree about the permanent employee. We have narrowed the field down to the one I mentioned. I just want to clear this up because I think the hon. member for Van-couver-Quadra is not aware of the fact that the Minister of National Revenue did not single out the construction industry. They were exempt, and other people felt there was an unjust advantage to them; we were giving them something that others were not getting.
You mean you were taking something away from them by this directive?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
It is true of the working man who is not a permanent employee. The construction worker is now paying a tax on something it had not prior to this directive, that is true. But under the circumstances, as I have said, we are trying to find the proper approach to this thing. If we felt that this chap should not pay the tax, if directive No. 10 ought to be withdrawn and the tax exemption granted, we would be in a position then perhaps of having to grant

similar exemption to a great many other people who have been paying tax on this for a great many years.

Probably the only practical difference between the superintendent and the carpenter would be that the superintendent would have 12 months work and the carpenter would only have nine. In cold, hard fact, I think in most cases that would be the only difference. The carpenter would work for nine months for this company and then he would not get anything else for three months in the winter. Then, he would go to work again in the next year. I do not think the distinction the minister is drawing is a very fair one. I think the two men are actually in the same category.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext:
There are lots of other
points.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: There are a considerable number of companies with a great many persons on their permanent payroll who are not superintendents, but mechanics and carpenters. There are a number of these people. Therefore, it is not fair to suggest that construction companies generally have a small nucleus of people of a permanent nature in the higher income brackets, if you will, who enjoy benefits that others do not. There are a great many people in the large centres of Vancouver, Toronto, Montreal, and all the other cities, who have permanent places, and these they agree to pay the year around in the first place, and they do, and they are carried over the months when there may not actually be employment. One of the reasons they do that is to keep their organizations functioning with that group of people. I should think my hon. friend would be in favour of that exemption rather than suggesting that it is not a fair one.
I am suggesting that it should be extended to cover the others.

I was most interested in the remarks of the Minister of Finance. I am going to take his own suggestion and direct a question to the Minister of National Revenue. That was the minister's advice. In the construction industry-I am not discussing superintendents or draftsmen, I am discussing the electrician, the carpenter, the steamfitter, the plumber, the steel worker- what is the definition by the minister's department of a permanent employee?

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext:
That is not very hard to answer. There are an awful lot of yardsticks by which a permanent employee is put in that category. For instance, is he eligible for pension benefits? Ordinary temporary employees are not. If he gets to the position

where he is permanent and is getting a salary, sometimes they are put on a minimum salary. We do not recognize them for pension benefits unless the pension benefits are applicable to all employees.
In the construction industry that is mostly with the union, and not with the company.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: That may be, but I would suggest to you that that is one of the yardsticks. A man is a permanent employee if he is head of a certain department; he may be the head man on the works; he may be the head man on construction, the head man on steel erection, and so on. The companies themselves know what their standards are when they designate a man as a permanent employee; and when it comes into us that that John Jones is getting a salary of $5,000, $8,000 or $10,000 and he is a permanent employee of the company, we accept their designation.
I thought there was something crazy about this entire matter, and now I know it.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: The hon. member is smart.

In other words, the Minister of Finance did not mean to, but he has been trying to lead us down a completely crazy path. Acting on his advice, I have asked the Minister of National Revenue what he means by a permanent employee, and he said it was easy; that there are some yardsticks. He has named the yardsticks, which means what? It means something that does not touch one-half of 1 per cent of those engaged in the construction industry. Therefore, all of this-I do not know just exactly what to call it-is eyewash that we have been handed. That is exactly what it is.
It does mean that the regulation brought in by the Department of National Revenue, as far as income tax is concerned, covers practically everybody in the construction industry of Canada if they are working away from home. If you are in the construction industry, sir-and I was for some time; that is where I started, as a matter of fact when I went to work-you are not a permanent employee unless you happen to be on the administrative staff on an annual salary basis. The plumbers, the steamfitters, the carpenters, the steel men are employed under trade union agreements on an hourly basis, and what the minister said a few moments ago did not include them in any way whatsoever. The minister said they were permanent employees if the employer said they were employed at $5,000, $6,000 or so much a year. Construction men are not employed in that way except in a very few
Income Tax Act
supervisory categories. I was very hopeful for a few minutes, from what the Minister of Finance said, that the majority of construction workers would be free of this regulation if they could show, as I took it from what the ministers statement said, that they were permanent employees; but after listening to what the man who collects the money had to say I think we have to point out that the majority of the men on construction, if they happen to be away from their home residences, are going to be caught by this regulation on the matter of board and lodgings.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: Nobody denies that.

I was interested in what the minister said, that sometimes when you go out of town on a job you get extra money. That is correct, but you pay for it in income tax. We are discussing one issue only, and that is a person being charged income tax on the actual amount of board and lodging.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: Which is equivalent to money.
It is not completely equivalent to money. That may be the attitude taken by the Minister of National Revenue.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: How much of it is?

I say there is something more than money, and that is human relationships, that is whether you are home or away from home; whether you are with your family or away from your family; whether you spend money once in a while to see your family or not. The sooner the Minister of National Revenue gets away from dollars and cents and comes down to human values, the sooner we will have a government that understands the situation, or what should be the situation, in this country.
I say, as one who either as a public representative or as a construction worker has been away from home a great deal, it is despicably unfair when a man is away from home, because it is required in the development of our country, because of his occupation, that he should be charged income tax on the actual board and room valuation away from home. I have not heard one thing yet from the Minister of National Revenue that in any way indicates he understands, or has even the slightest understanding, of the situation, or any desire to understand it. It is a matter of regulation, brought in under his power and his authority, and I hope that within the very near future, as he had the power and authority to bring it in, in the little time he has left with his power he will remove that same regulation.
I appreciate the fact that the Minister of Finance said what he did; that it was not something that required any amendment; it

Income Tax Act
was something done by regulation, something that was still, as I gathered it, under consideration, something upon which there are angles for and against. I expected that from the Minister of Finance, but I say that in view of what the minister said he should not have had this regulation made until everything had been weighed in the balance and he knew what was the right decision. The admission of the Minister of Finance himself, in which he put forward various problems and various aspects, is convincing evidence that a decision was made before all knowledge was forthcoming. I hope most sincerely, on behalf of those in the construction industry away from home,-and more and more will be away from home as Canada develops-there will be a change made immediately and made retroactively, that construction workers will not be charged income tax on their actual board allowances paid by their employers.

I would like to say a word on this subject. I would like to start out by admitting-and I think we all agree-that any individual's home living expenses are not deductible for income tax purposes. The reason for the payment of the living expenses and travelling expenses in the first place of a salesman or of any other individual is simply that there are out-of-pocket expenses incurred in order to earn income or salary. I can understand, as the Minister of Finance said, that there could be agreements, there could be conniving in some instances between employer and employee as to how much should be expenses and how much should be considered salary, and so on. I can understand where an individual or, shall we say, a person taxed as a single person, should not have these expenses deducted from his income for taxation purpose, but I cannot understand why anybody keeping up two homes, or keeping a family at home while he has to be away earning income and has to pay out-of-pocket extra expenses, should not be allowed those out-of-pocket expenses as a deduction from income for tax purposes. I think frankly the two-home idea, or the keeping up of a home by an individual at a place other than where he is earning his money, might well be the yardstick to follow.

Mr. Chairman, I think the importance of this matter can be gauged by the numerous representations made to the government regarding bulletin 10. I was quite amazed at the comments made by the Minister of Finance, because in the last few days I had wondered whether the department had seen fit to change its regulations, since I could not quite reconcile the facts as I know them with the picture presented to the committee by the Minister of Finance.

Let us get down to some specific example. I have taken from my files a particular example, which I think points up the absurdity of the position taken by the minister. In my province men engaged in construction work have done work 12 months of the year. They work, and they work regularly for a particular company. Many of them have worked for a great many years.
Perhaps they might get in seven months work this year and eight months the next year depending on weather conditions. Of course they are expected to live on the salary which they obtain over a period of perhaps seven, eight or nine months.
Let me illustrate my point by referring to a specific case. A constituent of mine works for a grain company. His job requires him to travel around the province of Saskatchewan building grain elevators, annexes to grain elevators and doing maintenance work for the particular grain company by which he is employed. This man has been working for this company for a number of years and as I say his job requires him to move about the province to a considerable degree.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: May I just interrupt the hon. member to ask if the gentleman to whom he refers is a salaried employee or a subcontractor?

I am not exactly certain how he is paid, but the man is working for a well-known grain company in this country. His foreman has appended a statement of the places in which he was required to work in the normal course of his job. I might say that in the last year for which he filed an income tax return he has worked in 15 different communities in the province of Saskatchewan for a total of 256 days. That constituted the basis of his salary for the year.
In the 1955 taxation year he received a total remuneration of $2,671 and he worked eight months that year. In the last taxation year he got in only seven months work. I imagine this was due largely to weather conditions over which neither he nor the company has any control and his total remuneration was $2,184. For the taxation year 1955 he submitted a claim for away from home expenses of $640 which amount was allowed and I think quite rightly so.
This gentleman is married and maintains a permanent home in Regina. In order to earn a living with the company for which he works he is required to travel around the province of Saskatchewan but he is not a casual employee. He works for that company for as long a period during the year as that particular type of work can be carried on and yet when he filed his income tax

return for the taxation year 1956 his total away from home expenses amounted to only $533.50 which I think you will consider quite reasonable in view of the fact that the man was away for a period of 256 days.
I do not think by any stretch of the imagination anyone could suggest that this man is claiming too much. As a matter of fact, one wonders just how these men are able to live away from home and submit claims for such modest amounts. The fact is that this year this man's claim was disallowed and he is being charged income tax on his away from home expenses. He still maintains his home in Regina and has a wife to support. This government expects that when he goes out to earn his living he is going to have to pay income tax on his actual expenses while away from his permanent residence. I have cited this example and I would like to have the minister comment on that case.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I do not think it is customary in the house to try to comment on individual cases. I am quite sure from listening to my hon. friend that if this chap is a permanent employee as we have discussed and is not some kind of contractor paid on a job basis, it would seem that the allowance ought to have been granted. But I do not think the hon. gentleman expects either the Minister of Finance or the Minister of National Revenue at this time to go into a case to find out if the circumstances would have justified that or not. Let us just talk about the principle involved.
I think I have made it clear, as has the Minister of National Revenue, that so far as we are concerned permanent employees of companies who work out of town are allowed expenses whereas non-permanent employees are not. I think my hon. friend would agree with me that we would only waste time discussing a particular case but I am sure my colleague would look at it to see if it was within that definition.

I was not dealing with this particular case with a view simply to obtaining justice for this one man. I am citing this specific example to illustrate the type of administrative decisions that are being made by the government. I certainly would not be satisfied even if the minister gave me his assurance that justice would be done in this single case because, as I say, this is merely an example and there are many other cases of this type. I think we should get down tc something we can get our teeth into, some example which points up the folly of the government's attitude toward this problem.
Income Tax Act
I know it is true in my own province and throughout the country generally that a great many employees do not work twelve months of the year. There are many who take on jobs which last only from early break-up in the spring until the frost sets in in the fall and yet these people are actually permanent employees even though they are perhaps not paid on an anual basis. Obviously if they are working for a company under a set of conditions which they understand when they accept the employment the company does not offer them an annual salary. Perhaps the companies should say, "We are going to pay you a certain annual salary." The amount of remuneration paid to the employee during the year will depend on the number of months he has worked in the locality.
In the illustration I cited the employee worked seven months one year and eight months the next so there was a difference in the annual remuneration he received. In this case I do not think it can be argued that the man is not a permanent employee. What I am suggesting is that there are many other cases like this. I do not want the minister to think that this case in itself is the end-all of this problem.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: No, but does my hon. friend not agree with me that whether or not he agrees with our principle-and I am ready to concede there is a wide difference of opinion about that-in the interpretation of the rule that we grant this exemption to permanent employees there will be some who will be found to be non-permanent employees? We cannot just say that all permanent employees will have a tax exemption and grant it on the assumption that he is a permanent employee. There has to be some decision.

I am not concerned about the definition of permanent employees. I would hate to think for a moment that the question of permanency was to be determined on the basis of the way in which the man is paid and that because he is working on an annual salary basis he is a permanent employee whereas if he works on an hourly basis he is not a permanent employee.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: As the Minister of National Revenue has told you, there are many definitions.
Yes, but it seems to me that most of the definitions he dreams up are designed to exclude taxpayers from receiving benefits under these regulations.

Hear, hear.

Income Tax Act

Many people who should be receiving consideration are not receiving it because the minister has enough of these jokers up his sleeve that he can always pull one out at any given time when an occasion arises.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: If you met a fellow for the first time and he told you that he was working for Jones and Company how would you find out if he is a permanent employee? What would you ask him?
I think the employers in this country are in a position to supply that sort of information.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: That is the answer.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: That is exactly what I told you.

I wish to bring out the point that there are a great number of cases where deductions have been disallowed; people working for reputable Canadian corporations or Canadian companies employing a great number of employees. That is not argument to suggest that because one employer, a small contractor, may hire one or two employees and may arrange something in order to meet these regulations that there is any reason why many thousands of Canadians should be excluded.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Agreed.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: Even in the government we have qualifications as to permanency. You are not made a permanent employee the first week you come in.
Even you are not.
Let us not confuse the term permanent employee.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: That is what you are doing.

You are referring to civil servants and the question as to whether or not they are permanent employees, but that has nothing to do with the question as to whether or not a man such as I suggest should be allowed deductions for time spent away from his home. This is not a question of permanency but should, I think, revolve around the question as to whether a man in the normal course of his job is required to be away from his normal place of residence.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I do not think my hon. friend really means that, does he? There are a great many people who do not have to leave their permanent place of residence.

That is quite true, but if John Smith is working for an electrical contractor, and it may well be that most of his work is being done in his own city, in his own home

town, and that contractor gets a contract to do the electrical work on a hospital in a town say some 200 miles away and the employer says to his employee, "We are moving out to this particular town in the early part of next week to get started on this new job and we may be gone for a month or so", that employee is away from his permanent residence.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: And he gets tax exemption.
Oh.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Because you just said that the employer said to the employee who is working for him, "We are going to the hospital to do a job" and so he gets tax exemption.

I just stated to my hon. friend right at the outset that there has been a case of an employee of a grain company whose job required him to be out of town during the construction season and yet his claim was disallowed.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I did say to my hon. friend a long time ago that we ought not to waste the time of this committee in trying to agree on a case in connection with which he is in possession of the facts and we are not. We do say that a permanent employee does get taxation exemption. My hon. friend may be arguing one particular case-
And many other cases too.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: All right, and many other cases too. The position was that he was not a permanent employee and that is a matter of complaint to the Department of National Revenue for that particular decision, but my hon. friend, a moment ago in a somewhat rhetorical manner, said that an employer said to his employee, "We are going out of town a couple of hundred miles to do this job and build this hospital." I am saying that if these employees are permanent employees- however you describe them-they do get tax exemption and let me add that a great many get it. Surely my hon. friend does not mean to suggest that we do not grant this exemption or that in fact a great many people do not get it?
Used to get it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
And are getting it now, right at this moment. I do not want to stop my hon. friend from presenting the case he has in mind at all, but if it is in detail I wonder if he would take it up with the Minister of National Revenue or his department, because we never do follow this practice of discussing individual cases. I did not at the outset suggest that we were out of order in talking about something that is not in the resolution, and I do not intend to do it now. However,

I would like to get this particular resolution agreed to and I think that the committee ought to accept my assurance that I recognize two things: firstly that directive No. 10 in so far as it relates to non-permanent employees is unacceptable to many people. I also recognize that there can always be differences of opinion as to interpretation of permanent employees but that is a matter of specific complaint about a specific case and not a general matter of amending the Income Tax Act.

This is not a question of a
specific case. As I pointed out several times to the minister, I have used this example because I think the use of one example will do a great deal to facilitate the debate or the discussion but I do insist that the fact that the minister has received so many representations from trade groups in all parts of the country, including groups from my own city, indicates that this dissatisfaction with directive No. 10 is very widespread.
The other point I would like to inquire into is this. Why was it found necessary to change the interpretation in connection with this administrative change which denied the man working on the same job and under the same working conditions exemptions this year, when he received those exemptions in former years? Who made the decision to make this administrative change-and why? That is the question I would like to have answered.

Mr. Chairman, I have
appreciated that all the Minister of Finance has said up until now has been almost restricted to the question as to whether or not one is a permanent employee and I think I know what is in the mind of the Minister of Finance in that regard. However I would like to carry it further, because I think it is completely wrong in all its aspects, not just on the definition of whether or not a person is a permanent employee.
I started in the construction industry when I was 17 years of age and I think I know it. If you are in the city of Vancouver and there is a job going on in Kitimat or in any other part of British Columbia, it is a big job, it is a union job. I stress that it is a union job. A certain contractor gets that job and he gets in touch with his own office and the men are sent out on that job for one month or two years; they are sent away from their homes or residences.
Such an employee may never have worked for that employer before. I worked for Hume and Rumble Limited for years and for C.H.E. Williams Company Limited, but if when I worked for C. H. E. Williams there
Income Tax Act
was no work for me-and that is where I served my apprenticeship-if the Hume and Rumble organization had a job 200 miles from Vancouver I might have gone into the union and they would have said, "There is a job for you 200 or 300 miles away from here for Hume and Rumble." Now I was not a permanent employee of Hume and Rumble but I was a permanent employee of C. H. E. Williams. I am saying it is wrong- being sent away on a completely new job, away from my home city, away from my residence and from my family-that I should be charged income tax on my room and lodgings while away.
I am not just discussing this on the basis of whether or not one is a permanent employee; I am saying that as far as I am concerned, in the construction industry since 1924 it has been basically wrong to charge a construction man away from his home income tax on his board and lodging. I hope you will consider it on the basis of principle and not just alone on the basis as to whether or not one is a permanent employee.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: May I just answer that point? I recognize the argument on principle, which perhaps the hon. member does not agree with, but with which the hon. member for Perth did, that perhaps this law ought not to apply to a single man. The hon. member for Vancouver East made his argument thinking of a married man who has a home from which he goes and to which he returns. That is a social ground. The hon. member even went so far as to suggest that on some occasions when he wants to go to visit his family perhaps his transportation costs ought to be considered as an expense-I do not know whether he went that far.
I did. If you are going to impose income tax on board and lodging you ought also to consider an exemption on the other side of the picture.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Quite so, and I appreciate the whole social argument that there is something to be said for an exemption to our general rule being considered because by the nature of the hiring in some cases, though not in all, when the workers live in the larger centres and have a permanent home there to which they intend to return. They do not wish, for instance, to return to Kitimat and live there permanently unless they decide to quit the job and settle down as storekeepers, or something of that kind.
The hon. member for Perth appreciated, perhaps, that this does not apply to the single worker. But this whole discussion has underlined the difficulty of arriving at a correct

Income Tax Act
solution. As has been pointed out, a great many construction workers are hired by the union, not by the employer. As one hon. member said, the employer indicates that he wants a certain number of men at a certain place on a certain date, and the employing union provides them. In the following year he may get a wholly different group. From year to year they may never work for the same employer twice.
I agree that this is unusual, though it is not a situation wholly confined to the construction industry. On the other hand, the basic fact is that we do charge income tax in other lines of industry on this kind of income. I think the hon. member appreciates my difficulty in arriving at a proper solution for these problems. I am free to confess that perhaps I should have been able to do it earlier than this. It is remarkably involved, in particular as to the manner of hiring which has been mentioned. If after full consideration we came to the conclusion that it might not be possible for a great number of these people ever to become permanent employees-
That ought to be pretty obvious right now.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
It is not obvious. The hon. member's peculiar situation in British Columbia is that there there is much more likelihood of finding non-permanent employment at the present time due to the present rate of expansion in the province, but this position does not exist to the same extent in other parts of the country, it is confined more to certain lines of industry or to certain union groups.
However, as I say, that is one of the circumstances that might be taken into account. The hon. member argues, in any event, that on social grounds it is desirable that full income tax should not be charged to men who are away from home because they ought to have a home life and be able to return home and have some money with which to do it. I recognize both these arguments and I can assure hon. members that the subject is not closed. It is one of the problems to which we have to find a proper answer, but I am not prepared to make any recommendation to the committee at the present time. I have opened my mind to the committee, and hon. members have been as frank with me. We have had full discussion with the employers and with the employees' union representatives, and I hope we can come up with an answer which will be fair to everyone.
I do not want to accept entirely what the minister has said with respect to this being, perhaps, a problem confined primarily to the province of British Columbia.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I did not say that.

I think this presents a real problem in some of the smaller centres and in some of the smaller provinces and, naturally, I am thinking of my own province where one finds employees going out to work on relatively small jobs.
I mention as an example a large number of bricklayers who were formerly employed in the brick manufacturing plant. That plant closed down, and those bricklayers now go all over the maritime provinces as employees of relatively small contractors building relatively small buildings, school houses, for example. When they have finished one job, they go to another. In no way could they be termed permanent employees. At least, they have not been called that in the past. They might work for three, four or five contractors during a year, and they are charged income tax on their expenses during that period. I really think that this puts men living in smaller areas at a greater disadvantage and imposes a greater penalty upon them than is imposed upon people living in larger centres.
For instance, I suppose that a bricklayer in Toronto may never have to leave his home town. He can work 365 days a year, minus Sundays on which you cannot work in Toronto, for a whole lifetime without paying for board and lodging outside his home. But if he is living in a smaller area which he has to leave to find work, this penalty is imposed upon him.
Also, possibly, it is somewhat ironic if one considers that a lawyer could perhaps devise a way by which this tax could be avoided. I am not sure what the position is today, but I know what the situation was six or seven years ago. I recall the case of bricklayers who went to Halifax to secure employment. They charged their expenses, but the Department of National Revenue disallowed them. They went to a certain lawyer, whom I know, in the following year and got advice, as a result of which they were not employed by the contractors at so much a day but were given a sub-contract to lay so many bricks. This brought them into the category of contractors. I know, because I happen to be the one who drafted the contracts, and after that they never had to pay any income tax, because income tax was not chargeable against a contractor, though it was against men working on the contract.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Should the hon. member be telling this? They will probably change the law now.

That was seven or eight years ago, and I should think that by now that loophole has probably been plugged. But when

a situation like that can develop it does suggest that there has been some inconsistency and that there is, as the minister has admitted, a problem here. I was glad to hear the minister say that it has not been determined as far as he is concerned, and I think he should reconsider this whole matter.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Before I call it six o'clock, would the minister indicate the business proposed for eight o'clock?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I noticed the hon. member for Vancouver East rising, and I hoped, if he was going to ask me a question, that we might continue. I indicated last night that I could not be here tonight; and we will go on with the excise tax resolutions.
And customs?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: And customs. But I would like to complete this part of the business so that tomorrow, when we go back to the income tax resolution, we can proceed with it.
Do I understand that the various sections of this act-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: We shall discuss those tomorrow, but I would like to feel that this part of our discussion had been completed so that we might not need to go back to this particular point.

I can put my question quite briefly. Is the present situation a matter of government policy, or is it the policy of the Department of Finance or a decision of the Department of National Revenue? I ask that because of the answer which the Minister of National Revenue gave to a question asked on February 19, to be found on page 1421 of Hansard, when the Minister of National Revenue said:
With regard to the other matters as to whether consideration is being given to the representation and the decision that has been made, these are questions for the Minister of Finance because they relate to a matter of policy.
I would like to be clear. Is it a matter for the minister, or who else is responsible? I certainly do not know yet.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I think I said at the beginning that the directive, known I believe, as No. 10, was set out by the Minister of National Revenue or under his authority.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Information bulletin No. 10.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Yes. I think it is correct to say he could send out information bulletin No. 11 altering that interpretation.
The reason that is so is because earned income is defined under the income tax law as including certain benefits, and this has been interpreted to include this particular
Income Tax Act
benefit. It is also the case that government policy, in so far as the amendment of the act is concerned, is in my hands.
And regulations under the amendment?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: No. So the answer made is quite correct, that if government policy were that board and lodging away from home should not be taxed, I would have to propose in the house an amendment to the Income Tax Act to say so. I hope I have made myself clear on that point.
Under whose authority was the change made?
This was brought in by a regulation. Therefore why do you require an amendment to wipe out a regulation?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Because up to that time, as my friend the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra has pointed out, board and lodging for construction workers away from home was not being taxed by way of income tax. That was also being done as a result of a directive many years ago. This directive altered that directive. So, as I say, another one in the future could alter this one.
Why not bring in another one now?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: For the reasons I have tried to explain for the last hour and a half, namely that I am not satisfied that the tax law can be made in such a manner that this fairly vexed question will apply across the board to most people. I do not mean taxes across the board to most people. I think that we can in fact arrive at a proper taxing system for benefits of this kind applicable to all those who ought to be taxed and not applicable to those who in our best judgment-and subject to the opinion of the House of Commons -ought not to be taxed. That is the position we are in today. As I have said, our conclusions are not firm. We were trying to work this thing out properly. I have not mentioned many other things, in the knowledge that these other things are in my hon. friends' minds as well as in my own and that we did not need to protract the debate, but I say that the matter must be thoroughly studied in order to try to improve the situation as we have it now.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: It being six o'clock-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: No, not yet.

I assure the minister that I am not going to take very long. From some of the things the minister said I am inclined to hope that this may be a case of things having to get worse before they can get better. I made reference to this matter in

Income Tax Act
my budget speech. I said I thought this bulletin which is under discussion was extending the discrimination that I have been attempting to draw to the attention of the minister at the budget stage for the last several sessions. I welcome the statement which the minister has made in part, because up until this year the only thing I have been able to get in the way of an answer from the opposite side of the house has been a few inconclusive words from the minister's parliamentary assistant on this subject. The one point to which I want to make reference, seeing that the discussion has gone this far, is this.
I agree in part with what the minister has been saying, namely that this problem is not something which is unique to the construction industry. As far as I am concerned, it applies equally, and as seriously, for example to the logging industry. In my opinion from the study I have made of the matter over the past several sessions, this whole question can be resolved only by a suitable amendment to the Income Tax Act, one that will remove what to me is a discrimination that now exists against the expenses that are incurred by those on wages and salaries in the course of earning a living. I think I have covered the particular points that to me are most important. I know that it is past six o'clock and I will therefore not say any more.

May I make a suggestion to the minister? May I suggest that he and the Minister of National Revenue give this question some consideration before the house sits tomorrow or, if they require further time, before the income tax amending bill is brought in. Then perhaps at that time they might be able to announce some change which will meet the situation. These representations today have been made in great earnestness, in the belief that there is an extremely serious problem which ought to be settled and that the department should send out a new directive altering the one which was sent out last year.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I am grateful to hon. gentlemen opposite for allowing us to continue past six o'clock. As I understand it now, we will proceed with the excise tax and customs tariff tonight. Should that business be completed, my parliamentary assistant will indicate what legislation might be proceeded with until ten o'clock. If it is not completed, we shall go on in the morning with whatever is uncompleted in excise tax and customs tariff and then we shall revert to income tax.
Succession duty?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Yes; and then we shall revert to income tax.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: For the information of myself and the chairman, may I ask the minister whether he is referring to the Excise Tax Act only or the Excise Tax Act and the Excise Act?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Both.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: In which order.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Excise Tax Act first.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
AFTER RECESS

The committee resumed at eight o'clock.

speakerposition: subtopic
