speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to make a few very brief general remarks about the Excise Tax Act, with sales tax features, because I think it is a matter of great importance. I should like to recall to the memory of the committee that in his budget speech of two years ago the Minister of Finance announced that he proposed to invite a small committee, including experienced persons in the business world, to study this technical problem with us and to make recommendations. I have in my hand a copy of the report of that committee, to which I should like to refer very briefly. I believe that it has not been possible yet, in any comprehensive way, to give effect to the report of the committee and, therefore, having regard to the background and the fact that the minister has asked for this report and that he got it, I am going to make some very brief references to it. I would ask the parliamentary assistant if he would be good enough to sum up in a general way what the situation is, and let us know where we stand.
So far as the detailed changes that are proposed this year are concerned, they are not very sweeping. I would be glad if the parliamentary assistant would indicate to us, if it is possible to do so, whether they in any way fit into a scheme, either that outlined by the committee or otherwise. As I said, I wish to refer very briefly to the report of this committee which is entitled, "Report of Sales Tax Committee, Ottawa, January 1956". It is addressed to the minister. It refers, first of all, on page 11 to the fact that there are three general levels in the marketing process; (1) manufacturer to wholesaler; (2) wholesaler to retailer and (3) retailer to 82715-192
Excise Tax Act
consumer. The committee makes this observation immediately following:
For the purpose of sales and excise tax levied at the manufacturer's level, it is unfortunate that ail goods do not follow these steps. Manufacturers not only sell to wholesalers but also to retailers and direct to consumers. Wholesalers sell to consumers as well as to retailers.
Now, I skip over some pages and then refer briefly to some recommendations in the report. I shall ask your leave, Mr. Chairman, to come back to the report perhaps later, but in the meantime I would refer to a few of the recommendations. The first recommendation is found on page 14:
1.	The existing scheme of valuation be continued for the present with statutory sanction.
2.	Selling price receive a statutory definition.
I shall not take the time of the committee to read the details of that, but just refer to the fact that it is made. Then I go on to recommendation No. 10 which says:
10.	The act contains over 25 references to the minister's discretion. In our views most of these discretions should be replaced by rules of law or by conferring authority on the governor in council to issue regulations.
11.	At some future date after suitable preparation and explanation to the taxpayers, the basis of the tax be changed from the manufacturer's level to the level at which retailers purchase goods. This is the level used for tax purposes in Australia. It follows that the broader base will produce increased revenues at the same rate.
Then, I go on to another later paragraph which refers to appeals. One of the strong points which the committee makes is the necessity of making appeals available, and I read section 19:
In our opinion the following matters among others should be subject to appeal: (1) Valuation (2) Non-arms-length transactions (3) Exemptions (4) Status as manufacturer (5) Penalty assessments.
We recommend that section 57 and subsequent appeal provisions of the act be rewritten to give effect to the foregoing.
Then, I should like to quote briefly from the general sections of the report:
For the purpose of this report we have received submissions from the organizations listed in appendix B and from a number of individual taxpayers.
I may say that the organizations listed in appendix B are very formidable looking. They include such organizations as the Canadian Chamber of Commerce; Canadian Construction Association; Canadian Electrical Manufacturers Association; Canadian Drygoods Association and so on.
In most cases, the persons or organizations concerned have appeared and our records contain transcripts of the evidence and discussions.
We have visited Washington and Australia and are forwarding to you a memorandum of our findings at these places.
I have just given the sketchiest outlines of this report. I have done so really to

Excise Tax Act
raise this important question and I hope the parliamentary assistant will give us a brief summary of the situation as he sees it. This sales tax is of tremendous importance, and I hope he will at least give us the general situation. The minister asked for this report, he got it and it is very far-reaching and comprehensive.
I hope that we may have a brief discussion on the far-reaching points which are raised in this report, and that we may at least have an idea of what the thinking of the Department of Finance is, or, at any rate, to what stage they have progressed in their pondering of this report.

There is one matter I wish to bring to the attention of the minister and that is the sales tax on drugs and therapeutic apparatus for the sickroom. I am perfectly sure that if this matter were thoroughly understood-and I am aware of the fact that it has been brought up in the house before- some relief would be given to those people who have to buy drugs. It will be understood that at the present time some new drugs are becoming pretty expensive. As I understand it, the sales tax is put on at the wholesale level, but nevertheless it is reflected in the price the consumer pays for his medicine. It does not seem fair to me that a person who is ill should be paying a tax in general for people who are well. You can buy the newer drugs in tablet form, but they are extremely expensive. I have talked to the people who own drug stores and they tell me they find it difficult even to convince some people of the high price of these drugs. Sometimes they show them their wholesale rate, but people generally do not understand that there is a 10 per cent sales tax at the wholesale level, and that the druggist reflects that tax in the cost of the goods to the consumer. The same argument applies to the therapeutic apparatus that is used in the sickroom. While a reduction was given in the last budget, I do not think it touches the problem at all, because a person with a chronic illness is paying that high sales tax all the time on the kind of drugs he finds it necessary to use.
I find it peculiar that certain things were taken off the sales tax list, such as edible gelatine, flavouring extract, meat tenderizers, salad oils and sandwich spreads, and that sort of thing. I do feel that this matter of tax on drugs and on therapeutic apparatus used in the sickroom should receive some consideration. The relief given in the budget does not cover these things. The whole matter should receive consideration and some relief should be given. I again draw the attention of the parliamentary assistant to
[Mr. Macdonnell.l
those unfortunately ill people and to those who are chronically sick, the people who pay taxes for the people who are well.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I should like once more to support the plea made by my friend, the hon. member for Lanark. The parliamentary assistant knows that this request has been made by members in various parts of the house on a number of occasions. I hope that the parliamentary assistant will bring to the attention of his minister the strength of our feeling that there should not be these taxes on necessary drugs and medicines. I understand that in some instances we have products which are subject both to customs duty on entry into the country, and then the sales tax on top of that. Obviously, with the pyramiding that goes on, one can see how high the prices of some of these articles become. I hope that in the discussion that will follow the parliamentary assistant will tell us whether the sales tax is still applied to wheel chairs, to hearing aids, to eye glasses, and things of that sort that are necessary for the health of our people. Surely a government that for these many years, shall I say for these several decades, has been professing an interest in the health of our people should not continue to put taxes on these necessities.

Mr. Chairman, with respect to the goods on which excise tax is collected, I am particularly interested in the article having to do with the making of showcards and signs of a non-permanent nature, namely those of cotton, paper or cardboard used for advertising bazaars and so forth. The interpretation that the department puts on this particular regulation appears to be that where the silk screen process is used the sign should be taxable as such. The fact is, that in most instances the sign painter today finds it more economical actually to use the silk screen process in the making of signs in instances where possibly only 50 or 100 such cards are used. For that reason they are not actually manufacturing. It would take a good deal of time to make 50 or 100 signs by lettering them by hand. The department does say that if they were hand-lettered they would be non-taxable. The fact that time is taken to make a screen and use it for just one particular purpose, because it is not likely that the date of a bazaar would come at the same time each year, or on the same day, should be taken into consideration. Actually I see very little reason for the ruling that the department has seen fit to employ in some particular instances. It is true, possibly, that if the silk screen process were used in the manufacture of many thousands of signs, the sign painter should come under this

tax, but where signs are used in such a small way it does appear to me to be rather undesirable to tax him.
I also find in most instances that it is the smaller manufacturer of the signs who is affected, the man who does not do a great deal of this work. He may be just beginning in this field, and naturally enough, not only is it difficult for him but it brings about a certain loss to the bazaars and other media which are employed for the purpose of helping the community.
One other question that arises is the duty charged on a celluloid type of sign which is not made in this country and which uses fluorescent paint which can be obtained only in the United States. It is a transparent sign that uses fluorescent paint. The particular sign I have in mind was used to advertise the campaign of the united good neighbours in the city of New Westminster, which compares with the community chests drives in some areas. The proceeds of the drive go to charitable organizations. The work is done gratuitously. It seems to me that in such instances the sales tax and the excise tax should not apply.

Mr. Chairman, before the
parliamentary assistant or the minister replies to the various matters which have been raised, one by my friend from Greenwood, on the general background of the sales tax, which is a very important matter, and the others which have been referred to by my friends from Lanark and Winnipeg North Centre with respect to the sales tax on drugs, which I think all hon. members are fairly well in agreement with, I would like to draw the parliamentary assistant's attention particularly to one subparagraph of the Excise Tax Act, namely, that dealing with potted, flowering or bedding plants, dormant flower bulbs and cut foliage.
They may seem to be a very insignificant matter in dealing with an over-all budget running into billions of dollars. However, it is something of importance to many in the florist, horticultural and nursery business in this country. Incidentally, Mr. Chairman, I may say, and I suspect your memory goes back almost as far as mine, there is something about this particular item which is vaguely reminiscent of what I think was popularly called the Dunning budget of 1930. I remember at that time there was a reduction in the customs duty on the importation of cut flowers and also on cast iron pipe. Some of us who perhaps were a little bit juvenile and a little smart-alecky toured the country thanking Providence that the government had seen fit to reduce the duty on cast iron pipe so we could hit the government over the head with it, and had reduced the duty on cut flowers 82715-192J
Excise Tax Act
so we could buy the flowers for the funeral. Both results, Mr. Chairman, you will remember were achieved in the election of 1930. It may be that the reduction of the sales tax on flowers on this occasion may augur the same happy result which was achieved in the election in 1930.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: You are too optimistic.
Well, hope springs eternal in the human breast, I might remind the minister, and sometimes it is justified.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: The happy result you referred to did not last long.

To be specific again I would like a clarification on the terminology used in section 1(f). There is a reference there to cut foliage. Does that mean cut flowers? I looked up the word "foliage" in the dictionary and I find it means leaves or flowers with leaves and so if the department follows the Oxford dictionary or any of the standard dictionaries they certainly are exempt providing the flowers have leaves on them.
There is some question about this, as you know. For instance, in my own constituency there is a grower who was selling tens of thousands of cut gladiola. Representations have been made to the department over the past few years. I had hoped that they were successful because though I am not certain I am told that the only primary product which today bears the impact of the sales tax is this matter of flowers and bulbs.
Bulbs are also included in section 1(f). I am wondering if in the future those who sell gladiola bulbs will be exempt from the payment of sales tax or not.
The situation is complicated, as I understand it, by the fact that if you sell less than $500 worth you are not liable to sales tax and therefore a part-time producer or a road-stand salesman who keeps inaccurate records may sell more than $500 but he escapes the incidence of the tax.
The total revenue which the department derives from this is negligible in terms of the over-all budget of Canada. I think it amounts to approximately $1 million a year. I am not for a moment adopting the attitude, "what's a million", but I think it is a very small part of our total over-all budget which amounts to billions of dollars. The cost of administration has been high. I would hope that this matter would be clarified and also I would like to see the term "nursery stock" clarified.
I know, as does the Minister of National Revenue, that there has been a great deal of discussion in the last few months with respect to the growing of certain flowers outdoors

Excise Tax Act
in my own constituency. The argument of the growers has been supported by the horticultural council and the experimental farm here in Ottawa that if flowers are grown outdoors they are nursery stock and therefore are exempt from sales tax because as I understand it nursery stock is exempt. But on the other hand, they are plants and it has been suggested that since they are plants they do not constitute nursery stock despite the fact that they are grown outdoors and therefore are not exempt.
The irony of it all is-and I am sure this will appeal to those who have been brought up in the Annapolis valley where temperatures are so much different from those in the rigorous climate of Ottawa-that according to the department whether a plant is nursery stock or not depends on whether it can survive the rigours of the Ottawa climate; in other words, if it can survive on the experimental farm here. This applies despite the fact that over 90 per cent of all nursery stock in Canada is grown in Nova Scotia, southern Ontario and British Columbia.
It would appear that there has been a tremendous amount of complication and difficulty in administering this section. I had some reason to believe that this new amendment would clarify this situation in that cut flowers, bulbs and other flowers which were grown outdoors but which were sold for the purpose of propagation would be exempt from sales tax in the future. When the time comes for the parliamentary assistant to reply I would hope that he would give us a fairly clear and concise explanation of what is included in that section. I hope he is not going to disappoint me by suggesting that the words are in keeping with the definition in the dictionary.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to make a few comments along the same line and concerning the same section referred to by the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings. I look forward with interest to the explanation of the term "foliage" and am interested in knowing whether or not it means cut flowers.
There are one or two other words in the section which require some clarification. There is reference to potted, flowering or bedding plants, and dormant flower bulbs. A bulb, strictly speaking, means a scaly root as in the case of a lily bulb. If we stick to the ordinary meaning, the word "bulb" would not mean a gladiola or tulip bulb, one of which is a corm and the other is a tuber. I have no boubt these were intended to be included but under the strict interpretation of the term "bulb" they most clearly would not be included.
[Mr. Nowlan.l
Section 1 (f) refers to "potted flowering or bedding plants." Does that mean that potted bedding plants are to be free of tax or do they have to be potted flowering bedding plants? I do not know. I know that some bedding plants have flowers and some do not.
There is also a question concerning the term "bulbs". If you stick to the strict interpretation of the term, does that mean a bulb such as a tulip bulb that one gets in the fall or would it include those in flower pots that you get now? In one part of the sentence in that section it refers to dormant flower bulbs but on the other hand it says that potted plants are free. There seems to be a distinction made and I am not sure what it is.
To get away from the subject of potted flowering plants for a moment I would like to mention briefly that I agree wholeheartedly with the remarks made by my colleague the hon. member for Lanark and my friend the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre respecting the removal of the tax on certain drugs and medicines. Indeed, a tax on articles such as medicine and drugs seems ridiculous and there can be no excuse for retaining it. If there is one I would certainly like to hear it.
The final thing I would like to mention has to do with the excise tax on cigarettes. At the present time on a 33 per cent package of cigarettes the grower receives 3 cents, the manufacturer receives 12i cents and the government receives 17 \ cents. Every year for a period of several years past the growers and manufacturers of tobacco have sent briefs to Ottawa and have come to see the Minister of Finance about reducing the excise tax on cigarettes and every year they are well received with a broad smile and are told, "We will consider it", and they go away with high hopes. But this year they went away with the highest hopes they have ever entertained. In fact, they were confident they would receive a reduction in the tax on cigarettes but as has been the case every year they did not get it.
The tobacco industry in southern Ontario is having many difficulties at the present time, particularly with regard to the marketing of its product. I realize of course that I cannot deal with that subject under this heading and I do not intend to attempt to do so, but regardless of what marketing method is used by the growers of tobacco a reduction in the excise tax on cigarettes would help the industry generally, both the growers and manufacturers.
In addition to that, as has been demonstrated by figures that have been shown to the

Minister of Finance by the association-I have a copy of them and I know other hon. members have-if the excise tax on cigarettes were reduced it would not lower the total amount of tax the government acquires from the industry at all. In fact, it would make very little difference, if any. At the same time if the excise tax were lowered it would help the industry generally and would probably help use some of the unused land in southern Ontario which at the present time is waste land because it will not grow any remunerative crops except tobacco. In addition to helping the growers of tobacco, the manufacturers and the industry generally, a reduction in the excise tax would help Mr. John Q. Public.
When one describes an article as a necessity of life one generally thinks of bread and water, I suppose, but I think in our modern civilization what would have been considered a luxury a few years ago is now considered a necessity.
These things are relative to the standard of living which we enjoy. It is quite clear that a loaf of white bread which is considered a necessity in Canada would be a luxury in a place like India, for example. So it goes with the standard of living, as the standard changes.
Many people may not like to think of tobacco or cigarettes in particular as being a necessity within the strict interpretation of the word as normally used. However, I think they may be considered as such because a very large percentage of the population in Canada smokes cigarettes every day. This is becoming increasingly so. Since the sales tax was removed on bubble gum, coca cola and other things, including pickles, prunes, pie filling and all the rest of them, it seems to me that it certainly would not have hurt the government, especially in view of the arguments presented, to have cut the excise tax on cigarettes. Five cents may have been too much to hope for, but three cents would have meant that we could have bought a package of cigarettes for 30 cents instead of 33 cents.
I have always understood that one of the main principles of taxation is "the ability to pay" theory but that certainly does not apply to the excise tax on cigarettes because not only the people in the upper income brackets but also those in the lower, and even the lowest income brackets, use cigarettes. Whether you like to think of cigarettes as a necessity or not, they are generally so considered by those who use them.
With regard to the "ability to pay" theory of taxation, this tobacco burden lands on the wrong group. It is the same thing as a tax on sugar, tea and coffee. The government took
Excise Tax Act
the sales tax off tea and coffee but made no change in the excise tax on tobacco. This again is a thing that hits the little man and I think the government certainly could have done something to help by cutting the excise tax on cigarettes by at least three cents, to help the industry, to help the grower of tobacco and to help the consumer, popularly known as John Q. Public. I believe the excise tax on cigarettes, in relation to the tax on similar things, is away out of proportion and I certainly think the government should consider reducing it.

I would just like to ask one or two questions in regard to the printing produced by schools or universities. I wonder just exactly what this means because if it was printing done by a school and just used by that school there would be no transaction at all. Does this mean it is printing that is produced for somebody else?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Done by themselves.
Well then if it is done by themselves for themselves there has been no transaction and this item is unnecessary, is it not?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: It would be a manufacturing process and would require a licence.
Not to print on their own premises, surely?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Yes. Any manufacturing over a certain annual value.
You do not think you could print for yourself without being a salesman, do you?

What I am
getting at is this: I know of one particular school where they do their printing of programs and one thing and another, and I do not think they ever pay taxes on that.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: There is a provision of exemption if a small total quantity is produced, I think in the regulation it is below $3,000; any producer or manufacturer whose total product for the year is less than $3,000 would probably not require a licence under the sales tax act.
Would potted plants include geranium slips that are sold by the thousands?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: If it is a plant and not a cut flower yes.
Well, is it a plant?

A geranium slip is not a plant; it might come under foliage. A geranium slip very seldom has

Excise Tax Act
any leaves on it but comes in bundles, sometimes 25, 50, 100, and the hot house man might buy 2,000 or 3,000 or even 10,000 at a time. They run at different prices according to the quality and the different species, and if they are new species they have to pay that much more. Now I just wonder if they come under this heading?
Mention was made of cigarettes and I mentioned this last year. My angle on this was that it not would help sell the cigarettes here in Canada but it would stop smuggling and we still have a great deal of smuggling going on in this commodity. I think if the tax had been reduced a little it might have helped, because there would not toe the incentive for the smuggler to bring them into Canada.

I would just like to ask one question of the parliamentary assistant with reference to resolution 1 (d) on page 9 which suggests that the sales tax should be repealed on gasoline-powered self-propelled trucks, mounted on rubber-tired wheels, for off-highway use exclusively at mines or quarries, and complete parts thereof. I am wondering if this is the only class trucks under consideration.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
We already have
exempted the diesel-powered trucks for similar use and it was felt that these gasoline trucks should be put on a par with them.

These are for off-highway use exclusively at mines or quarries and I am wondering, for example, why this particular category has been singled out and why the same provision should not apply to logging on off-highway use.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I think we will recheck that. I am quite familiar, of course, with the exemption with respect to mines, because it did have an effect on the very large diesel trucks that commenced operations a few years ago. My advisers tell me that they will check with respect to use in logging.

Mr. Chairman, I would like to revert to the discussion which was commenced by the hon. member for Peterborough with respect to 1 (c), printing produced by a school or university when for its own use and not for resale. If my memory serves me well, the parliamentary assistant said that unless a plant produces $3,000 worth of printing in a year it is not required to obtain a sales tax permit and consequently its goods are not eligible for the sales tax. However, here we have a place where a school or university has its own plant-now that may be merely a mimeograph machine, a multigraph machine, or it may be an actual printing press. If it

produces these goods for its own use it does not pay sales tax. The sales tax now runs at 10 per cent, but if that same school or university purchases its printing requirements from a printing plant, it pays the sales tax-is that not correct?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: That is right.

Now what is fair about that? What are you trying to do? Is the department trying to urge schools and universities to put in printing plants to be run by their own students and thereby undercut the printing establishments of the community?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: No, Mr. Chairman. It is for the small amount of printing that is now being done by those schools who have-
But it has to be $3,000 worth-if it is a small order less than of $3,000 worth they are not eligible for sales tax anyway.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Relatively small. We did something of this nature for churches, you will recall, a couple of years ago; in the matter of the production of their calendars and so forth.

Oh no, the parliamentary assistant is wrong. What you did with regard to the production of calendars was to take off the sales tax where they were produced by printing plants. You have not done that here. If I remember correctly, it would be May or June last year. What you did was to take off the sales tax on calendars or church papers or service papers, as the case may be, when they were produced for churches, taking into consideration that churches are nonprofit making institutions. In this case you are saying that the sales tax shall be removed if the goods are produced within the school or the university. What you are doing is trying to encourage schools and universities to put in their own printing plants. Isn't that true?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Most of them have such arrangements now, and it has been a matter of petition by them that this kind of production was subject to tax.

It is subject to tax, if my memory serves me well, in that they paid sales tax on 220 per cent of the cost of the paper, or some such amount. A limit was set, and I think it was 220 per cent of the cost of the paper which was used. Nevertheless, if they did not have an overall production of $3,000 they paid no sales tax in any event, so if they used more than a certain amount-take 220 per cent at $3,000, and you have about $6,600 worth of paper-they were eligible for

sales tax, but if they used less than $6,600 worth of paper they would not be taxed in any event.
They were "liable", not "eligible".

All right, they were
"liable". What do I care so long as they paid the tax. The point is that there seems to be a trend here to force schools, universities and eventually, I suppose, commercial enterprises to instal their own printing equipment, whether it be duplicating, mimeograph, multigraph or any other type of reproduction equipment, or whether it be to use their own employees to man an actual printing plant. There seems to be a trend to give them an advantage over established printing houses within their communities. Just precisely what is the intention?

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: This change is brought about to help schools. Take, for instance, the situation in Toronto. For some years they had to pay a sales tax amounting to upward of $30,000 on their printing. Now the printing is done by the board of education for all the schools in Toronto which come under its jurisdiction. The cost is billed out to them, and in their method of accounting it is shown as having been received by the schools from the central printing office. The Toronto board of education urged upon the minister and the Department of National Revenue the inequity caused by the former system and the extra expense which it represented for education, an expense which amounted last year to over $30,000, according to my recollection. In order to relieve them of that bill and make a contribution toward education we thought it would be advisable to take the tax off printing done in schools for their own use.

At long last the Minister of National Revenue is beginning to see the justice of removing the sales tax from supplies to municipalities. It is just too bad that he did not see fit to go further and remove the tax altogether from supplies to municipalities. All he has done in this resolution is to encourage the schools and the universities to instal their own printing plants.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: What is wrong with that?

The minister says in
effect that if you buy your printing from a local printing plant you must pay sales tax, but if you instal a printing plant in your school you do not pay sales tax. Who are you trying to do out of a job, I ask you? The printers in the new municipalities? Are you trying to staff your schools with pseudoprinters? Are you trying to say: so long as you mimeograph this stuff you can get out
Excise Tax Act
of sales tax, but if ever you give the job to a local printer outside the board of education this is going to cost you 10 per cent more?
If the minister does really have the cause of education at heart, and if he even gave a thought to all the people engaged in printing in this country, he would have said that all supplies to boards of education should be exempt from sales tax. That is what he should have said.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext:
I would like to ask the hon.
lady if she is in favour of this change or not.

I am not, in its present
form.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext:
Would she prefer to see
the tax continued, and the schools taxed to the tune of 10 per cent?

They have had that all
along.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: Oh, no, if a school purchases its printing supplies from a small establishment which is doing business of $3,000 or less-
Who could live on $3,000? Don't be stupid.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext:
Hamilton and Toronto are
not the centre of the world. There are lots of places-small municipalities-where there are printing establishments who print bills and the like which do not do more than $3,000 worth of business. They do not have to take out a licence and they do not have to pay tax. But if, on the other hand, the school deals with a larger firm-I do not know the names of printers in Toronto, and they charge sales tax, the tax would be added on to the cost of what they purchase for a particular school.
In Toronto the situation there is that they have a printing establishment which does an enormous amount of work, as is apparent from the figure of $30,000 which I have mentioned-and that would probably mean $500,000 of actual printing. This establishment employs printers, not students, and the schools get the benefit of this tax concession when the material is distributed and billed out to them, that is, to the schools which come under the board's jurisdiction in the city of Toronto.

The minister knows full
well that all he has to do is introduce a resolution saying that supplies to boards of education shall be exempt from sales tax, and that all they have to do is to provide their printers with a certificate saying that the work is exempt from the tax, after

Excise Tax Act
which they would get their supplies free from this imposition. I say that the present proposal is iniquitous and that it is simply an encouragement to school boards, small or large, to establish their own printing plants so that they might be exempt from this 10 per cent sales tax which they would otherwise have to pay if they bought their printing from any printing shop in their localities. Because it is a fact that any printing shop which does not do $3,000 worth of printing in a year is not a printing shop.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: There are lots of them.

Who can make a living
out of that? Do you mean someone with a little press in the kitchen? Don't be silly. How much revenue could people make out of $3,000?

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext:
That is not all of it. That
is on job printing.
Certainly, job printing. Do you think anyone makes a living out of $3,000 worth of job printing in a year?

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: I never contended that.

That is what you have
been saying.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: On job printing you don't have to pay tax, and, another thing, Mr. Chairman-are you through, madam?
No, I am not through.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext:
Another thing is that we
could do as the hon. lady suggested and take the tax off altogether. But that is not government policy.
You're not kidding.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext:
Do not forget that sales tax
is on a great many things for the purpose of raising revenue; and in many instances where you have in the schedule certain exemptions we believe that by relieving of the sales tax it cuts down in a good many instances the cost of production. There are a great many people in this country who do not pay any other tax than the sales tax. I have always contended that the sales tax or a certain measure of it was one of the just taxes and one of the taxes that produced revenue. With all of the demands that are being made, you cannot run this country without revenue. You must get it from some place. You can divide it among income tax, corporation tax, succession duty, excise duty, sales tax and all the rest of it.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: But no capital gains tax.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext:
You will see in the years to come that same principle will be followed

because you just cannot run the country without taxes and without money. It is taxes that make the clock tick.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Tick-tock.
At least the Minister of National Revenue has said in effect what we have been saying all along.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: We have not accepted your view.

Oh, no, you do not believe it if we say it. But you have said it yourself. You say it here now. You are saying this: "We are taxing everybody who makes $1 in this country" or "we are taxing everybody who buy $1 worth of goods in this country because we think it is right and proper that the person who goes in and buys a dollar's worth of goods should pay into the federal treasury". That is precisely what you have just said.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: That is the principle upon which it is founded.

That is very interesting. The minister has just said that is the principle upon which it is founded. We have said that in the field of duplicate taxation municipalities should be exempt from the sales tax upon their purchases and we have said this repeatedly.
For years.

Now the minister brings in a resolution, obviously intended as a sop to a certain small class, which says that if you do your printing in the cafeteria or whatever other place you may have, in a school or university where you can slip in a mimeograph machine, you shall not pay sales tax. The only persons who would ever have had to pay sales tax would have been those schools or universities which use up $3,000 worth of paper at the 220 per cent rate to produce their supplies. Otherwise they were exempt anyway. Hence when the minister starts to talk about little places here and there, may I tell him that he does not touch them at all.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: They are free already.

That is right, they are free already, as the minister says. So now he has got into the larger field of the boards of education which use large quantities of printing and which have heretofore bought that printing from recognized printing establishments which, I presume, used organized labour. Why did he not go one step further and say that any supplies printed for schools or universities would now be exempt from sales tax? Why did he put it

in this way, namely that the printing plants must be within the schools or universities or they would not be exempt? Why did he not go the extra step and say that anyone who supplied printed material to boards of education or to universities would now be exempt from sales tax? That is what he should have done. Why did he not do it?

I wish to say a few words on that same question, following up what I requested earlier. In the regulations of 1954 I find something to which the hon. member for Hamilton West referred. At page 16 of the regulations I read as follows:
Where persons, firms or corporations produce printed, multigraphed or mimeographed matter for their own use, to a value of over three thousand dollars per annum, they are required to account for the consumption of sales tax on their total production of such goods. The tax is to be computed on the total cost of all materials (including electros, engravings, stereotypes), plus 220 per cent.
That would bear out what the minister had to say a while ago in respect of the $3,000. However, it strikes me, that the situation is as well indicated just now by the hon. member. Just how many printers can you find-those who are legitimate printers-in this country who can possibly get by upon $3,000 worth of job printing a year? I do not know where the minister could find them. I am sure there would be many little printers in this country who would be only too happy if the minister could show them someone who can live on doing $3,000 worth of printing a year. As far as the small printer is concerned, his plea is that he should be entitled to at least $6,000, and that this $3,000 is completely unrealistic.
To follow through on what the hon. member has just said, the minister indicated that the Toronto school board paid $30,000 in taxes. Does he for a moment pretend to tell us that the city of Toronto can find a sufficient number of small printers who do less than $3,000 a year so that the school boards in that area could let their work out by tender to all these various places or just give them to the small printing establishments doing less than $3,000 a year. I do not believe there are enough in the whole country who are doing $3,000 a year and less.
The fact is that it bears out this plea I made earlier here in respect to silk screen processing which comes under the same regulations. As I understand it, these small printers, because they are actually too small, are being unnecessarily deprived of jobs which they would normally get. They come under $6,000. Yes, you find many of them but not certainly those who do $3,000 a year or less. Just off the record I would ask 82715-193
Excise Tax Act
the minister if he can name one single individual printer in this country who makes his living on $3,000 worth of printing or less.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: I never contended that that was their only method or their only work. I personally know of small printing establishments which run a small newspaper but their job printing does not exceed $2,000 a year; and it is on the job printing that they would pay the sales tax. They are not required to take out a sales tax licence on that account. I do not know how long ago that law was changed in that regard but that is what has been in effect for a number of years.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: That came in in 1951, I believe.

As far as I am concerned, the point is this. How many of these small printers would a school board such as the Toronto school board or the Vancouver school board be expected to let this work to in the way of the small printer? They must be job printers of that size. I do not believe there are a sufficient number. We are actually forcing the school boards to go into the job printing business-
Certainly.

-in order to take advantage of this same regulation that we have at the present time. I should like the minister or the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance-whoever wishes to do so-to indicate to me why some of these signs that we cannot get in this country and are compelled to import from the United States are taxable either under the duty or the excise tax as the case may be and the sales tax as well, such as the one I indicated here.

It is a little difficult to sit here and find that most of the previous speakers have discussed the topics which you intended to discuss. I was listening to the hon. member for Oxford as he listed the candy, cokes and motor cycles affected by this budget and I was wondering if we were going to call it the zoot suit or Elvis Presley budget. It seems those are the articles chiefly covered in it.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: By the way, where is everybody tonight?

I thought that might be an appropriate remark because of the famous visitor in the district.
I have been listening to the remarks of the hon. member for Hamilton West and she was touching on a rather sore spot so far as the government was concerned. There seem to be some signs of faltering steps towards

Excise Tax Act
removing the burden of double taxation which faces the home owner in the municipality. I was especially interested as well in finding that the Minister of National Revenue indicated his agreement with the fact that of every dollar spent his department gets its percentage. Of course that is not the case when you get down to the municipal level. I might say to the parliamentary assistant that I have no apologies for speaking along these lines again tonight.
There is some indication here that we are trying to remove this double taxation. In the first section of the resolution there is a reference to precast concrete shapes when purchased by municipalities for bridges in public highway systems; structural steel when purchased by municipalities for bridges; desks and chairs specially designed for use in classrooms. Then, in section 2, on the following page, there is a reference to equipment specially designed for use directly in road making, road cleaning or fire fighting, and things of that kind.
The situation, of course, which faces the home owner is this. He earns his weekly wage and the dominion government removes its share at the time he receives it. The government does not lose any time in doing that. In the United States when a home owner pays his personal income tax to the department he is allowed to deduct the amount of his municipal tax bill from his total income for the purpose of computing his tax for the year. This, of course, is not done here. Some of the dollars which have not been taken by the federal government then are paid over to the municipality and we have a situation where these municipal tax dollars are taxed again by this dominion taxing authority when the municipality makes a purchase to carry out its various projects, whether it be road building or fire fighting equipment.
This reminds me that we seem to be always in the position where the government is backing up to a little better situation all the time. At the start we had the position that the government did not pay any tax on federal buildings. Then we got it down to a 4 per cent assessment basis, and after some hammering it was dropped to 2 per cent. Then, after some more hammering this year we got it down to zero, a begrudging recognition that there is a serious problem facing the municipalities.
I think we Should suggest to the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance, and to the Minister of National Revenue who is in the house tonight, that here is an opportunity to follow along the lines of the suggestion made by the hon. member for

Hamilton West. Surely, a municipality could be furnished with a sales tax exemption certificate the same as that which is provided to industry. Perhaps there might be some items on which it would be impossible to calculate the amount of the tax; those would be small purchases, I think. The sales tax licence could be quoted in connection with major purchases by municipalities, the same as business enterprises do. In that way, we would remove this burden from the municipality and we would again make it a little easier for the home owner. We would be taking steps towards spreading out the tax base of the municipality in somewhat the same manner as it is spread out in connection with collections by the federal government, as referred to by the Minister of National Revenue tonight. These are steps that I feel we have got to take and the sooner we take them the better for the whole economy.
I would wish that there would not be such reluctance, such a slow backing up, when we in the opposition make these requests. When the parliamentary assistant answers he might perhaps tell us just how much the loss would be to the federal treasury if some such system as this were brought into effect. Surely the total purchases of the boards of education in the country would be known and how much sales tax would be lost if that source of revenue were not available to the federal treasury. Surely the purchases of the municipalities of these various items must be known, and how much revenue the federal treasury would lose if some such certificate were used. Sooner or later, either the government faces the problem this way or it must bring the provinces back to Ottawa to sit around the table again to properly divide up the tax base.

Could the Minister of National Revenue or the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance tell us approximately the number of schools which are able to produce printing for themselves and also the number of universities? I ask that because it would seem to me to be very unfair if say four universities out of the total number in Canada could produce their own printing and the rest could not. There is also unfairness in respect of schools. I would think that very few schools in Canada could produce their own printing.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: A lot of them do.

But there must be quite a number that do not. Surely there is discrimination there, in so far as the schools themselves are concerned.
The school which cannot produce its own printing has to pay a sales tax and the other

does not. I would imagine that one of the departments has obtained these figures and it would be very helpful if we could be given them this evening, or is this a shot in the dark, based on the representations received from one or two boards of education.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: We have had representations from a lot of schools and from members of parliament.
Could we be told what information the government has on this?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: No; I have asked and we have no statistics as to the number of universities and schools that would be involved. We have no statistics on them; we have records of those that pay taxes, but we have not analysed them. A great number of representations have been received urging that this was a tax they would appreciate having relief from.
What would be the loss to the treasury if all of the printing purchased by schools and universities were exempted from sales tax? Has there been any estimate made of that figure?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: No estimate made, no.

I just want to ask a question on this. The Minister of National Revenue said that the school board does the printing. If the school board did the printing, then under this item it would not be covered, according to the way I read it. It says:
Printing produced by a school or university when for its own use and not for resale.
Would you not have to put in there, "by a school or university or school board" to cover places not under the board's control?

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: The school cannot do it itself; it is the management of the school that does it.
It does not say that in this paragraph.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: It is common sense.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: That thought occurred to me. I think between now and the time of the bill we will get some legal advice on it.
It is something that should be added because it is not clear.

I would like to supplement the question asked by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra to this extent. Can we have the full picture? After all, why should school boards go into the business of printing any more than into the business of plumbing? Can we find out the extent of 82715-1931
Excise Tax Act
this? Might I suggest to the parliamentary assistant that it be understood that this item be left over until we get further information about it, and get a clearer picture of the situation as it is?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, we know that this is a relieving section. I am sure my hon. friend would not want to deny the people who benefit from this sales tax exemption. Certainly as far as statistics are concerned I would think only the educational associations would have that. We have not got it in the bureau of statistics. There is no special item for something of that kind.
I believe the Minister of National Revenue said that representations had come from the city of Toronto. Therefore, I presume the city of Toronto has its own printing plant?

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: That is right.
That is the board of education?

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: Yes; that was our information.
The board of education of the city of Hamilton does not have its own printing plant.

It will have to buy its
own printing plant.

That is precisely it. My hon. friend says that the Hamilton board of education will have to buy a printing plant. Therefore in order to gain a 10 per cent relief, boards of education will have to establish their own printing plants because the city of Toronto wants 10 per cent relief. Is that the situation?

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: You can draw that conclusion from it.
There are only four cities in Canada which are going to benefit. All the other boards of education are either going to have to buy their own printing plants or still pay the 10 per cent.

I just want to direct this question to the parliamentary assistant. Do I understand now that we come into this house, and he comes in with his experts with a plan to exempt all of these items, but he is not in possession of figures to tell us how much the treasury will lose? Is that the plan? Will the parliamentary assistant say tomorrow, "You people are not going to have to pay this from now on; we do not know how much it will cost the treasury, but you are free anyway?" Is that the position we are in?

Excise Tax Act

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: No; on most items of some consequence of tax loss, from statistics in the Department of National Revenue, we are able to give some idea of the amount of revenue that the crown is willing to forsake by a reduction in taxation, but this is not an item in that category; it is not one of substance.
Then, we can expect the answer is that possibly when we come to section 1 we will know how much is involved in dealing with paragraphs (a), (b) and several of those paragraphs. Is that right?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Several of them.

Unlike the hon. member for Hamilton West, I am not opposed to this particular assistance for the schools but I do feel that all schools should be able to take advantage of the 10 per cent reduction in the sales tax or excise tax, as the case may be. As I see it, the only way to make all schools eligible on the same basis is to make it possible for them to receive a rebate, or not be charged with tax in the first instance when they have a printing job done for them by a printing establishment. If it were done in that way our job printing establishments would be able to carry on as they are today, but our smaller schools would not of necessity have to purchase large printing presses to carry on the work or get the benefit of the tax alleviation that some of the others are to get.

I think this is ill thought out legislation. In the first place, the dominion government has taken the big end of the tax collecting privileges from the municipalities and the provinces. We all know that the municipalities are the children of the provinces. The municipalities pay excise taxes on everything they purchase. There is only one fair way to do it and that is to make exemptions for municipalities, including school boards.

I would like to say a word or two on the subject of price. I notice that the resolution reads;
Resolved, that it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Excise Tax Act and to provide, among other things,
The part to which I should like to refer just briefly is part VI, "Consumption or Sales Tax." Under paragraph (f)(ii) we find:
. . . without limiting the generality of the foregoing, any amount charged for, or to make provision for, advertising, financing, servicing, warranty, commission or any other matter.
The thing that I am particularly interested in is the word "financing". I feel that the word "financing" should apply only to that part of

the money that is used in the manufacture of the article, the financing of the operations. I believe the tax is now charged on the financing of the sale of the article, provided the manufacturer or someone dealing at less than arm's length carries on the financing of the sale of the article. But if the finance corporation carries the finance charges instead of the manufacturer, then there is no sales tax on the financing. The manufacturer must borrow the money to finance it in the first place and he has the necessity to finance the charges; on top of that he is going to have to pay the sales tax on the finance charges or the consumer is going to have to pay the sales tax on the finance charges. I think the word "financing" there should be made to refer only to the finance charges in the manufacturing of the article and not in the sale of the article.

Mr. Chairman, I would like to say one word further with respect to this matter of printing to which reference has been made by the hon. member for Hamilton West, the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra and others. Certainly there is something about this which I think would warrant further study and investigation. We have a provision here that educational institutions, schools or universities which produce their own printing for their own use and not for resale are exempt. Well, that is an advantage undoubtedly to many educational institutions, and to that extent we are all for it; we welcome it. But why should there be a differentiation made between the large educational institution or university, shall we say the University of Toronto or McGill, and the small institutions? I am not sure, of course, whether the University of Toronto or McGill has its own printing establishment but obviously some have. Hereafter they can print and not pay sales tax, while smaller ones such as Acadia, Mount Allison, St. Francis Xavier, Dalhousie, or St. Mary's-and I can call the roll all across Canada-which have not any printing establishments-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Do they not do mimeographing and other types of printing?

Is this the Ontario complex? Is the parliamentary assistant suggesting that smaller universities shall be content with mimeographing and the universities of Toronto and McGill shall have printing? I think a university, whatever its size may be, is entitled to the same treatment so far as the taxation authorities are concerned, whether it does mimeographing or printing. I think that this section should be redrawn so that goods which are supplied to these institutions should be exempt from the sales tax. It is no good for the parliamentary assistant to say, "Well,

if they buy from an institution or a printing plant which does less than $3,000 worth of printing a year they do not have to pay sales tax."
I come from a small town in this country, probably one of the smallest towns which is represented by a member-the town is not- and from which a member of parliament happens to come. We have one or two printing establishments in that town and they are not making any money. I do not think any of them is paying an excessive income tax to the Minister of National Revenue. But I am certainly sure they are all doing over $3,000 worth of printing a year, or they would not be in existence at all. Therefore, this exemption of less than $3,000 a year means nothing.
What is happening by this amendment is that the department is going part way to meet a situation with which it should have dealt realistically long ago. The printing of these national institutions should be exempt from sales tax. I am not sure who is responsible for carrying out this change, whether it is the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance or the Minister of National Revenue; but I do suggest and urge that further consideration should be given to this. Otherwise you are going to have the situation that printing done for the larger educational units in this country-all of which I know are carrying a heavy burden, but nevertheless presumably the larger ones are in a slightly better position to carry it than the smaller ones-are going to be exempt from the sales tax on their printing, whereas the smaller ones are going to be compelled to pay the sales tax because they do not own their own printing establishments. They have to buy their printing from some plant which I can assure the minister will not be one doing less than $3,000 worth a year. I again urge that this matter be given further consideration.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, first of all I want to support the suggestion made by a number of hon. members that a happy solution to this problem would be to provide exemption from the sales tax to all municipalities and school boards. If the government is not prepared to do that, I suggest that there is another way by which the problem might be solved. This suggestion arises from a little research I have been doing in some of the volumes that I have under my desk. I find that the Excise Tax Act, which in the main is for the purpose of imposing certain taxes, including the sales or consumption tax, has in it section 32, which reads:
The tax imposed by section 30 does not apply to the sale or importation of the articles mentioned in schedule III.
I find by looking at schedule III in a number of the volumes across the years that
Excise Tax Act
it has been growing in length. No doubt my friend the parliamentary assistant would like to boast of that fact, but in particular I would point out that the section of schedule III which is headed "Printing and Educational" has been growing in length year by year. I take it that what this proposed amendment would do would be to add another sentence or two to the printing and educational section of schedule III of the Excise Tax Act. I ask hon. members to note that quite a number of items are included in this section under the small capital heading, "Printing and Educational". I would like to give some of them, bibles, missals, prayer books, psalm and hymn books, religious tracts, Sunday school lesson pictures, books, bound and unbound, pamphlets, booklets, leaflets, scripture, prayer, hymn and mass cards, and religious mottoes, and pictures unframed, for the promotion of religion, and so on.
There is another paragraph which lists books, printed and bound, that contain no advertising and are solely for educational, technical, cultural or literary purposes, and so on.
There is another paragraph that starts off:
National manufacturing, industrial or mercantile trade directories.
There is another paragraph that starts off:
College and school annuals.
There is something else included in that paragraph and I will come back to it in a moment. Then I find magazines and such things as "manuscript, phonograph records and photographs", and so one. The item I said I would come back to is newspapers. When one thinks of the amount of printing that is done in this country surely the largest part of it must be in the printing of newspapers. I suggest to the government that this list is now getting fairly long particularly with bulky newspapers like-what one should I mention; I had better be careful-
The Winnipeg Free Press.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
No, I will refer to the Toronto Daily Star or the Sunday Telegram. When you consider the proportion of the printing in this country that is already tax free by virtue of the items that are listed in schedule 3 of the Excise Tax Act, isn't the solution simple? Why not exempt all printing from the sales tax After all, to a large extent the cost of printing is in labour content and what is being imposed here is a sales tax not on goods but a sales tax largely on labour.
I submit that if the government is not prepared to move as fast as it should in the matter of relieving the municipalities of

Excise Tax Act
the requirement to pay sales tax, at least it might travel in the direction in which it is already travelling, and since the government has extended to newspapers and the publishing of books and many other printed items freedom from the sales tax, why not wipe the slate clean and remove the sales tax from all printing?

Having had some little experience with the printing business, probably the committee would be interested to know that even in the case of those plants which produce less than $3,000 worth of printing in the year and thereby are exempt from sales tax, by reason of the fact they have no sales tax licence these plants are required to pay sales tax upon supplies which they purchase. Therefore the paper, ink and other products they purchase, by virtue of the fact that they do not have a sales tax licence, are subject to sales tax in their hands.
It seems to me that this is an empty sort of thing because even a school board which produces its own printing and does not thereby require a sales tax licence which would exempt its purchases from sales tax is forced to pay sales tax to its suppliers on the paper, ink and other supplies which it purchases to produce its own goods.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: The previous speaker said that was an inconsequential portion.

Well it may be inconsequential but this particular section then elevates this thing into a broader field. The minister said the board of education of the city of Toronto pays $30,000 sales tax a year. That would indicate that it buys $300,000 worth of printing. It takes a fairly sizeable plant to produce $300,000 worth of printing so what he is saying in effect is that the city of Toronto which is quite capable of installing a printing plant which could produce $300,000 worth of printing in a year shall be exempt from sales tax whereas a small town or city or an individual university such as those described by the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings must still pay sales tax upon the supplies which it uses.
The member for Winnipeg North Centre read from the act a list of various articles with respect to printing which are exempted from sales tax. Now those articles are exempted from sales tax regardless of who prints them, so if my memory serves me well I would think that the only things that are now taxable are simply the supplies which are used by the various boards of education and by the universities.
Educational supplies.

We are talking about educational supplies now. Therefore it seems to me that the minister should consider this particular clause and possibly he would agree to letting it stand until such time as we can consider how we will deal with it. Certainly in its present form it solves nothing. For the people who use very limited quantities of supplies it merely gives them a tax relief of 10 per cent of the total cost of their supplies and for those who use a large amount, that is to say, the big people who are in a better position probably to pay, it exempts them from the total cost of sales tax on their supplies. I believe that is grossly unfair. The scales are weighted in favour of the big fellow against the little guy and I personally am very much opposed to it.

Excise Tax Act

Mr. Chairman, may I ask the parliamentary assistant why cut flowers were not included. That again seems to be discrimination. These other products are exempted and cut flowers are not. They are difficult to market because there is such a large percentage of wastage and I am sure that there must have been representations made by florists from all over the country to the effect that cut flowers should be included as well as plants. Why has the department deliberately left out cut flowers and given exemption to the other plants?

I think it could be said that that, surely, is in the nature of an item of luxury. It is also the equivalent of something that is manufactured and produced in that form. Has the department no figures? Surely it must have some idea how much money is involved, and how much the tax on cut flowers has produced as distinguished from that on potted flowers, or potted plants or bulbs or cut foliage; what are the figures for these different items?

Is that in addition to the $700,000?

Mr. Chairman, I have been looking over this list and I find it is a very small list which does not cover what I was trying

Excise Tax Act
to talk about at all-artificial eyes, hearing aids, liver extract, vaccine for polio and so on.
The point I was making is that when you are charging for drugs, especially for some of these new drugs, you are imposing a tax on sickness. There is a whole field of these requirements, in addition to the articles which are normally used by sick people. The list I have in mind is a long one. You are making people pay a tax on illness to support people who are well, and the time when they are ill is the very time when they are not earning money. People suffering from chronic diseases are especially burdened by the taxation now imposed. It is true the tax is put on at wholesale level, but it is, nevertheless, reflected in the price charged to the person who is ill. I think this is a very unfair tax on any account. Certainly the list should be enlarged from its present puny length.
Can the parliamentary assistant not realize how ridiculous it is to send down to a drugstore for a hot water bottle for somebody who is ill and discover that there is a 10 per cent sales tax on it? Mr. Chairman, I want to ask one or two further questions to follow up my previous questions about this report on the sales tax, but, first, I want to make it perfectly clear to the parliamentary assistant that we are very dissatisfied still with this clause about printing and to suggest to him that no answer, so far as I can recall, has been made to the very clear statements which we on this side have made.

In concluding my statement of proposed tax changes I should report progress on consideration of the report of the sales tax committee. Careful study has been given to certain technical changes in the structure of the law, and I am confident that some of the deficiencies in the existing legislation can be corrected.
Now there you have, on the one hand, quite an admission in that phrase "some of the deficiencies can be corrected," yet on the

other hand there is no indication that I can discern here of anything being done. And we wind up with a blank negation, as follows: "but I do not propose to recommend any changes in the direction of basing the tax on the retailer's purchase price."
It was perfectly competent for the minister to say that, of course, but that was only one of a whole host of recommendations made by this committee which, as I say, was composed of able men who did not rush in without being asked, but who were asked by the minister himself to do the job.
I want to raise one or two questions which I think are worthy of answer because they touch upon very important issues. I draw attention to the fact that the minister, according to this report, has now 25 different discretions, and I suggest that this is a matter which certainly might have been looked into and that we might have had more than a mere casual reference to that. The minister-and let us approve his having done so-got competent people to make a report. As I have said before-and I say it most sincerely-there is never an item that comes up for discussion on a budget resolution that is not subsequently discussed by those officials and ministers who review the budget for the following year. On health items that also happens. Usually in tax matters relating to drugs and health the officials of the Department of National Health and Welfare are also consulted. There is sometimes a great deal of difficulty in just pulling out particular items of drugs because many of them pretend to have the same benefit, they are named and priced differently and their content of a certain drug element is different. There is great difficulty reported to us by the officials of all these departments
